transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Janine Herbst.
President Trump has tried a lot of things to bring down the high cost of gas and diesel.
Last week, announcing that Russia would provide tons of diesel,
which Trump says would bring down the prices at the pump.
But analysts say the amount won't really make a difference in the U.S. market.
Trump also removed recent sanctions against Russia.
NPR's Mara Eliasson has more.
The sanctions that Trump signed off on less than a month ago,
targeting Russia's energy revenues, which helped Russia fund its war against Ukraine,
now the U.S. is going to be adding to those revenues.
And Congress, with big bipartisan support,
passed a law just a couple of days before that giving Trump expanded tariff powers,
specifically in hopes he would use them to put more economic pressure on Russia.
Now he seems to be doing exactly the opposite thing.
NPR's Mara Eliasson reporting.
Ukrainian President Zelensky says his military is ready to stop attacking Russian oil refineries
if Moscow halts its own attacks on Ukraine's energy facilities.
NPR's Joanna Kikisas reports President Trump has lifted those sanctions on Russian oil
and he's demanding that Zelensky be replaced.
Writing on social media, Zelensky said any de-escalation of strikes
must be part of an energy ceasefire and backed by real security guarantees.
"The real cause of this war in Europe is Russia and Russia alone," he said.
Zelensky slammed Trump's decision on Friday to lift sanctions on Russian diesel.
The Ukrainian leader says this move will only prolong the war and kill more civilians in Ukraine.
On Saturday, Russian bombs killed at least 23 people,
including four children in apartment buildings in the southeastern city of Zaporizha.
Trump blames Zelensky for the war and says Ukraine must hold elections for a new president.
Joanna Kikisas, NPR News, Cave.
Hackers are ramping up attacks on critical systems, from the water sector to hospitals,
not with the help of AI.
And a collective of cybersecurity companies is calling on the federal government
to take action to defend those systems.
NPR's Jenna McLaughlin has more.
In July, Iranian hackers disrupted water systems across the United States.
Meanwhile, the Government Accountability Office recently revealed
that many federal agencies don't even know what operational technology,
the tools that monitor physical processes like water pumps, is connected to their networks.
Companies in the Operational Technology Cybersecurity Coalition
are urging the government to mandate basic cybersecurity standards
for federal civilian agencies when it comes to these kinds of critical systems.
Tatiana Bolton is the coalition's executive director.
Right now, federal agencies are operating with massive blind spots.
She says the government needs to designate federal officials with accountability
and segment networks for security.
Jenna McLaughlin, NPR News.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
Police in India have freed the leaders of a movement
that's calling for protests surrounding the controversial revision of voter rolls,
even as they call for more demonstrations.
NPR's Diya Hadid reports it's the latest political crisis
to roil the government of Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
The release of the three men came a day after they were removed from their airline seats
and detained by police just as their flight touched down in the capital.
They were among the thousands detained on Saturday
as security forces tried to stave off protests.
The forces barricaded parts of downtown Delhi,
cut off the internet in parts of the city,
shut down metro stations and railway lines and ban gatherings.
Still, protests play.
Demonstrators are demanding the resignation of the election commissioner
after a revision of voter rolls struck off more than 130 million people
or forced them to justify why they should be allowed to stay on the rolls.
The Prime Minister has not addressed the controversy.
Diya Hadid, NPR News, New Delhi.
Hurricane Simon, a Category 4 storm with maximum sustained winds of 150 miles an hour,
is churning just off the coast of Mexico and the Pacific,
and it's expected to move inland later today as an extremely powerful storm.
Forecasters say Simon could bring 10 to 20 inches of rain
over parts of the southwestern part of Mexico,
and the National Hurricane Center says flooding and mudslides are possible.
The popular tourist destination of Puerto Vallarta
boarded up windows on businesses, stores and hotels.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.

topics.text: Trump removes recent sanctions on Russian energy revenues while touting Russian diesel supply
Zelensky offers to halt refinery strikes if Russia stops attacks on Ukraine's energy facilities
Hackers target US water and hospital systems; coalition urges federal cybersecurity standards
Indian police free opposition movement leaders ahead of protests over voter roll revisions
Hurricane Simon, a Category 4 storm, nears Mexico's Pacific coast with heavy rain forecast
